raw_response:
I am 65 years old, and I have been farming my land in Quzhou County for over four decades. My education has taught me to read, observe, and not waste money on inputs that do not pay back. I have six mu of good flat land on the North China Plain, and I know this soil better than my own hands. The groundwater table has dropped over the years, and fertilizer prices keep rising, so I manage carefully.

This year, I will stick to the rotation that has fed my family and paid for my children's schooling: winter wheat followed by summer maize. I do not gamble with new crops like stevia or cotton — the market is uncertain and the labor is too much for one man at my age. Wheat and maize have stable demand, the dealers come to the village, and I know exactly how to grow them.

For the wheat, I will sow in early October after rotary tillage to break up the corn stubble and level the field. I use an improved semi-dwarf variety — it stands well against lodging and responds to fertilizer without growing too tall. I will apply about 32 jin of pure nitrogen per mu, split between basal and topdressing at the jointing stage, plus compound fertilizer for phosphorus and potassium. I will irrigate three times: the critical winter irrigation to protect against freeze, one at jointing, and one at grain filling. Three pesticide applications will be enough — herbicide at sowing, one insecticide spray in spring, and a fungicide if the weather turns humid.

For the summer maize, I plant immediately after the wheat harvest in mid-June. I use a hybrid variety with good drought tolerance and dense planting adaptability. I will not till — direct seeding saves time, fuel, and moisture when the summer heat is fierce. Maize needs less nitrogen than wheat on this soil because of the residual fertility, so I will apply about 20 jin of nitrogen per mu through compound fertilizer. Two irrigations will suffice if the summer rains cooperate, and I will spray three times for weeds, borers, and leaf diseases.

I expect 500 kg per mu from the wheat and 600 kg per mu from the maize. These are conservative estimates — I would rather be surprised on the upside than disappointed at harvest.
